questions.question: What is the fundamental goal of statistical language modeling?

options.text: To maximize computer CPU clock frequency
To estimate the probability distribution over sequences of words or tokens
To render 3D computer graphics from text
To translate machine code into assembly language

questions.explanation: Language modeling fundamentally assigns probabilities P(w1, w2, ..., wn) to sequences of words or tokens.

questions.question: In an n-gram language model, the Markov assumption states that:

options.text: The probability of a word depends only on the previous n-1 words
Every word is completely independent of all context
Words have infinite long-range dependencies across chapters
Word order does not matter at all

questions.explanation: The n-gram Markov assumption approximates the probability of the current token by conditioning only on the prior n-1 tokens.

questions.question: Which classic smoothing technique handles zero-probability unseen n-grams by reallocating probability mass?

options.text: Kneser-Ney smoothing
Gradient descent
Backpropagation through time
AdamW optimization

questions.explanation: Kneser-Ney smoothing is a renowned technique that accounts for the continuation probability of unseen n-grams.

questions.question: What limitation of traditional Bag-of-Words (BoW) models do distributed word representations (Word2Vec) overcome?

options.text: BoW ignores word order and treats words as orthogonal one-hot vectors with zero semantic similarity
BoW is too slow to execute on modern computers
BoW cannot represent punctuation marks
BoW requires deep transformers with millions of parameters

questions.explanation: BoW one-hot vectors are orthogonal and cannot represent semantic relatedness (e.g., king - man + woman = queen).

questions.question: The Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) architecture in Word2Vec predicts:

options.text: The surrounding context words given a single target word
The target center word given its surrounding context words
The sentiment score of an entire sentence
The next paragraph in a document

questions.explanation: CBOW predicts the target center word from context tokens, whereas the Skip-Gram model predicts context from the target.

questions.question: What problem plagued standard Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) when processing long text sequences?

options.text: Vanishing and exploding gradients making it difficult to capture long-range dependencies
Inability to run on CPU processors
Inability to work with floating point numbers
Instant overfitting on single sentences

questions.explanation: Standard RNNs suffer from vanishing and exploding gradients over long unrolled recurrent steps.

questions.question: How do Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks address the vanishing gradient problem?

options.text: By removing all non-linear activation functions
Through gated memory cells (input, forget, and output gates) maintaining constant error carousels
By processing all sequence words simultaneously in parallel
By ignoring all past context tokens

questions.explanation: LSTMs use explicit forget, input, and output gates along a continuous cell state line to preserve gradients.

questions.question: What is perplexity in the context of language model evaluation?

options.text: The exponentiated cross-entropy loss measuring how surprised the model is by test data
The speed at which tokens are generated per second
The total number of parameters in the neural network
The percentage of misspelled words in training corpora

questions.explanation: Perplexity is exp(cross-entropy); lower perplexity indicates the model assigns higher probability to ground-truth tokens.

questions.question: Why can standard RNNs and LSTMs not be parallelized across time steps during training?

options.text: Because they use GPU acceleration
Because calculation at step t depends sequentially on hidden state h_(t-1)
Because text datasets have irregular line endings
Because they do not have weight matrices

questions.explanation: The sequential recurrence relation h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t) prevents parallel forward and backward computation.

questions.question: In Word2Vec Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS), what does negative sampling do?

options.text: It samples noise words to train a binary logistic regression classifier efficiently without calculating full softmax over vocabulary
It discards all negative sentiments from sentences
It removes grammatically incorrect words from text
It inverts matrix values during backpropagation

questions.explanation: Negative sampling avoids the prohibitive expense of normalising over the entire vocabulary by sampling k noise words.

questions.question: What is the primary role of an embedding layer in neural language models?

options.text: To compress text into a single integer
To map discrete vocabulary indices into continuous dense vector representations in d-dimensional space
To translate English words into French
To format output text with HTML styling

questions.explanation: Embedding layers map high-cardinality discrete token IDs into dense semantic vector representations.

questions.question: Which loss function is universally used to train autoregressive language models?

options.text: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
Cross-Entropy Loss (Negative Log-Likelihood)
Hinge Loss
Kullback-Leibler divergence with zero prior

questions.explanation: Autoregressive models maximize the log-likelihood of target tokens, equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy loss.

questions.question: What is the difference between static embeddings (like GloVe) and contextualized embeddings (like BERT)?

options.text: Static embeddings assign a single vector per word regardless of context; contextual embeddings assign representations based on surrounding tokens
Static embeddings can only be used on GPUs
Contextual embeddings do not use vectors
Static embeddings require 100x more parameters

questions.explanation: Contextualized representations dynamically disambiguate words (e.g., bank of a river vs. money bank) based on context.

questions.question: Who introduced the Transformer architecture in the landmark 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need'?

options.text: Yann LeCun et al. at Meta
Vaswani et al. at Google Brain and Google Research
Geoffrey Hinton et al. at University of Toronto
Demis Hassabis at DeepMind

questions.explanation: Vaswani et al. introduced the Transformer architecture in 2017, revolutionizing sequence modeling.

questions.question: What is the mathematical formulation of Scaled Dot-Product Attention?

options.text: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(Q * K^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V
Attention(Q,K,V) = sigmoid(Q + K + V)
Attention(Q,K,V) = ReLU(Q * V^T) * K
Attention(Q,K,V) = norm(Q - K) * V

questions.explanation: Scaled Dot-Product Attention multiplies Queries with transposed Keys, scales by 1/sqrt(d_k), applies softmax, and weights Values.

questions.question: Why is the dot product scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) in Scaled Dot-Product Attention?

options.text: To invert negative weights into positive values
To prevent dot products from growing excessively large for large dimensions, which would push softmax into regions with tiny gradients
To ensure total sum of weights equals zero
To reduce RAM consumption on GPU chips

questions.explanation: Scaling prevents large magnitude dot products from causing vanishing gradients in the saturated tails of softmax.

questions.question: What is the primary motivation for Multi-Head Attention over single-head attention?

options.text: It reduces total parameter count by 50%
It allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions
It removes the need for feed-forward layers
It eliminates the need for GPUs

questions.explanation: Multi-head attention lets different attention heads focus on distinct linguistic relations (e.g., syntax, coreference, semantics).

questions.question: Why are Positional Encodings necessary in Transformers?

options.text: Transformers have no built-in recurrence or convolution, making self-attention inherently permutation-invariant without position signals
To ensure sentences have an even number of characters
To encrypt tokens before sending across the internet
To translate token embeddings into audio frequencies

questions.explanation: Because self-attention operates as a set-to-set function, positional encodings must explicitly inject token order information.

questions.question: Which of the following is a relative positional encoding method popular in modern LLMs like Llama and Mistral?

options.text: Sinusoidal absolute positional encoding
RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding)
ASCII character index addition
One-hot sequential encoding

questions.explanation: RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) encodes relative position by rotating key and query representations in complex space.

questions.question: What is the difference between Pre-LN (Layer Normalization before sub-layers) and Post-LN Transformers?

options.text: Pre-LN stabilizes gradient flow through residual connections, making deep models easier to train without warm-up
Post-LN is only used for speech recognition
Pre-LN requires three times more memory
Post-LN eliminates all attention layers

questions.explanation: Pre-LN routes the residual path directly without normalization, preventing gradient decay and improving training stability.

questions.question: What is the role of causal masking in decoder-only Transformers (like GPT)?

options.text: To blur out profanity in training text
To prevent attention from looking at future tokens (positions > t) during autoregressive generation
To compress the model weights into 8-bit integers
To force the model to translate text backwards

questions.explanation: Causal masking sets upper-triangular attention logits to -infinity so position t cannot attend to subsequent future tokens.

questions.question: How does FlashAttention optimize the self-attention operation on modern GPUs?

options.text: By quantizing all matrix values to 1-bit weights
By tiling computation and recomputing attention on-chip in fast SRAM to minimize high-bandwidth memory (HBM) IO bottlenecks
By replacing all matrix multiplications with addition operations
By skipping every alternate token in the sequence

questions.explanation: FlashAttention reorganizes attention computation to minimize slow memory transfers between GPU HBM and SRAM.

questions.question: In the Transformer architecture, what constitutes the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) block?

options.text: Two linear transformations with a non-linear activation (e.g., GeLU or SwiGLU) in between, applied position-wise
A recurrent LSTM gate loop
A 3D spatial convolution filter
A random forest ensemble

questions.explanation: The position-wise FFN consists of two linear projections with an activation function like GELU or SwiGLU.

questions.question: What distinguishes encoder-decoder models (like T5) from decoder-only models (like GPT)?

options.text: Encoder-decoder uses bidirectional attention on input and causal attention on target; decoder-only uses causal attention throughout
Decoder-only models cannot output text
Encoder-decoder models have no attention layers
Decoder-only models cannot be trained on GPUs

questions.explanation: Encoder-decoder models encode input prompts bidirectionally and generate output tokens autoregressively.

questions.question: KV Caching (Key-Value Caching) during LLM inference is used to:

options.text: Prevent retraining on updated Wikipedia articles
Store previously computed key and value states of prompt tokens so they don't need recomputation at each generated token step
Cache user prompts in local browser storage
Compress model weights into zip archives

questions.explanation: KV caching preserves K and V tensors across decoding steps, reducing inference time from O(N^2) to O(N) per step.

questions.question: What is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) in LLM tokenization?

options.text: An encryption standard for secure model weights
A subword tokenization algorithm that iteratively merges the most frequent pairs of bytes or characters
A lossless audio compression algorithm
A method to delete punctuation marks

questions.explanation: BPE is an iterative data compression technique that constructs subword vocabularies by merging frequent adjacent symbol pairs.

questions.question: Why is subword tokenization (e.g., BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) preferred over word-level tokenization in LLMs?

options.text: It solves the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem while maintaining a compact, manageable vocabulary size
It guarantees zero training loss in one epoch
It converts all words into emoji representations
It eliminates the need for embedding matrices

questions.explanation: Subword tokenization splits rare or unseen words into familiar subword pieces, preventing out-of-vocabulary failures.

questions.question: What is the typical objective function during the pre-training phase of an autoregressive LLM?

options.text: Next-token prediction (causal language modeling)
Masked sentence classification
Image segmentation regression
Binary sentiment analysis

questions.explanation: Autoregressive LLMs are pre-trained on massive corpora using the self-supervised objective of predicting the next token.

questions.question: What did the Chinchilla scaling laws (Hoffmann et al., 2022) reveal regarding compute-optimal LLM training?

options.text: Model parameter count should scale 10x faster than dataset tokens
Model parameters and training token counts should be scaled in approximately equal proportions
Training tokens should remain constant while parameters increase infinitely
Compute budget does not affect final model performance

questions.explanation: Chinchilla demonstrated that for compute-optimal training, model size and training tokens should scale equally (1:1).

questions.question: In pre-training data curation, why is deduplication of documents crucial?

options.text: To prevent the model from memorizing repetitive text, regurgitating private data, and degrading perplexity
To increase the physical size of SSD storage required
To double the compute power consumed by GPUs
To introduce random spelling mistakes

questions.explanation: Deduplicating training corpora reduces verbatim memorization, mitigates bias amplification, and improves sample efficiency.

questions.question: Which dataset was originally created by scraping outbound links from Reddit with at least 3 karma?

options.text: WebText (used for GPT-2)
Common Crawl
ImageNet
MNIST

questions.explanation: OpenAI created WebText by scraping outbound Reddit links with >=3 upvotes as a proxy for human curation.

questions.question: What is the 'curse of multilinguality' observed when pre-training cross-lingual LLMs?

options.text: Adding more languages without increasing model capacity degrades performance on individual high-resource languages
The model stops speaking any human language
GPUs cannot handle non-Latin alphabets
Word order differences crash the training loss to infinity

questions.explanation: When model capacity is fixed, allocating parameters across dozens of languages dilutes representation fidelity for each.

questions.question: SentencePiece tokenizer is notable because:

options.text: It treats the input text purely as a raw byte stream without requiring language-specific pre-tokenization or whitespace splitting
It only works on English text with Oxford commas
It deletes all numbers from training data
It translates input text into Python code before tokenizing

questions.explanation: SentencePiece treats whitespace as a regular symbol (_), providing universal tokenizer support across languages.

questions.question: What does synthetic data generation contribute to modern frontier LLM pre-training and post-training?

options.text: It exhausts GPU memory without producing tokens
It augments scarce high-quality reasoning and math datasets through curated, filtered AI-generated examples
It introduces guaranteed zero hallucination permanently
It eliminates the need for human safety audits

questions.explanation: High-quality synthetic datasets (e.g., textbook-quality examples, verified math proofs) enrich specialized reasoning capabilities.

questions.question: What is the Common Crawl foundation in LLM pre-training?

options.text: An open repository of petabytes of web crawl data used as the primary raw source for web text datasets
A proprietary Google database closed to researchers
A benchmark test evaluating LLM reasoning speed
A hardware protocol for connecting NVIDIA GPUs

questions.explanation: Common Crawl provides open web scrapes that serve as the foundation for filtered datasets like C4, RefinedWeb, and FineWeb.

questions.question: What is the primary role of data decontamination in benchmark evaluation?

options.text: Removing test set questions and answers from pre-training and fine-tuning corpora to prevent benchmark contamination
Scrubbing bacteria from server racks
Formatting text files to utf-8 encoding
Deleting all negative reviews from e-commerce sites

questions.explanation: Decontamination ensures test benchmark samples are not leaked into the training set, preventing inflated evaluation metrics.

questions.question: Which tokenizer token represents the start or end of a sequence in transformer vocabularies?

options.text: Special tokens such as <BOS>, <EOS>, or <|endoftext|>
Punctuation periods only
The uppercase character 'Z'
The escape key ASCII code

questions.explanation: Special tokens like <s>, </s>, or <|endoftext|> mark boundary conditions like sequence beginning and termination.

questions.question: What does PEFT stand for in modern LLM fine-tuning?

options.text: Parallelized Execution of Floating Tensors
Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
Predictive Error Filtering Technique
Pre-trained Embedding Fast Translation

questions.explanation: PEFT stands for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning, adapting large models without updating all pre-trained weights.

questions.question: How does LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) reduce trainable parameters in fine-tuning?

options.text: By pruning 90% of model layers entirely
By decomposing weight update matrices into low-rank factor matrices delta_W = B * A
By rounding all weights to 0 or 1
By training only the embedding layer

questions.explanation: LoRA decomposes the delta update matrix delta_W (d x k) into the product of two low-rank matrices B (d x r) and A (r x k) where r << d.

questions.question: In LoRA, if hidden dimension d=4096 and rank r=8, how do trainable parameters compare to full weight matrix W (4096 x 4096)?

options.text: LoRA trains 4096*8*2 = 65,536 parameters instead of ~16.7 million (~0.39%)
LoRA trains twice as many parameters
LoRA trains zero parameters
LoRA trains 8 million parameters

questions.explanation: Full rank requires 4096*4096 = 16,777,216 params, while LoRA factorizes into B (4096x8) + A (8x4096) = 65,536 params.

questions.question: What is QLoRA?

options.text: Quantum Computing LoRA
LoRA applied on top of 4-bit quantized base models using NormalFloat4 (NF4) and double quantization
Quick LoRA without backward pass
LoRA implemented exclusively in SQL queries

questions.explanation: QLoRA reduces memory footprint by keeping the frozen base model in 4-bit NF4 while training 16-bit LoRA adapter matrices.

questions.question: What is Prefix Tuning?

options.text: Adding learnable continuous virtual prefix vectors to the keys and values of every Transformer layer
Prefixing every user prompt with 'Please answer honestly:'
Deleting the first 100 tokens of every document
Converting all output text into JSON strings

questions.explanation: Prefix Tuning prepends learnable, task-specific continuous vectors to the Keys and Values across all attention layers.

questions.question: How does Prompt Tuning (Lester et al., 2021) differ from Prefix Tuning?

options.text: Prompt Tuning adds learnable soft prompt virtual tokens only to the input embedding layer, rather than every transformer layer
Prompt Tuning updates all model parameters
Prompt Tuning modifies only the last linear layer
Prompt Tuning cannot be used with transformers

questions.explanation: Prompt Tuning injects tunable continuous virtual tokens strictly at the input embedding sequence level.

questions.question: What is Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT)?

options.text: Training models on prompt-response pairs formatted as explicit instructions to follow user intent
Compiling LLM code into x86 machine instructions
Writing user manuals for neural networks
Teaching LLMs how to play chess only

questions.explanation: Instruction tuning trains base models on structured (instruction, input, output) datasets so they behave as helpful assistants.

questions.question: What is 'catastrophic forgetting' during full fine-tuning of LLMs?

options.text: The GPU loses power and drops unsaved checkpoint files
The model loses general capabilities and knowledge learned during pre-training when updated heavily on a narrow task
The tokenizer forgets punctuation marks
The model output becomes completely blank

questions.explanation: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when gradient updates on a specialized dataset overwrite foundational knowledge.

questions.question: What is Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) in the standard LLM post-training pipeline?

options.text: The first stage after pre-training where models are trained on curated demonstrations of desired assistant behavior
A technique where humans write code live in the GPU
A method to calculate corporate payroll
A training process that uses no labels or human data

questions.explanation: SFT fine-tunes pre-trained models on high-quality demonstrative dialogues before reinforcement learning alignment.

questions.question: Which library developed by Hugging Face is standard for training LoRA and adapter configurations?

options.text: peft
numpy
pandas
requests

questions.explanation: The Hugging Face `peft` library is the industry standard for configuring and training PEFT methods like LoRA.

questions.question: Why can LoRA adapters be merged back into original base model weights for zero-overhead inference?

options.text: Because matrix addition W_final = W_base + (B * A) is linear and can be pre-computed before deployment
Because adapters delete the original base model
Because LoRA runs in JavaScript inside the browser
Because GPUs don't support matrix multiplication

questions.explanation: Since W_new = W_0 + (alpha/r)*B*A, the products can be added directly into W_0, eliminating runtime latency.

questions.question: Full parameter fine-tuning of a 70B parameter model in FP16 requires approximately how much GPU memory for optimizer states alone (Adam)?

options.text: ~8 GB
~40 GB
~560 GB to 1 TB+ (due to 16 bytes per parameter across weights, gradients, and first/second Adam moments)
~10 MB

questions.explanation: Adam requires 8 bytes per param for moments + 4 bytes for grads + 4 bytes FP32 master weights = 16 bytes/param (~1.1 TB for 70B).

questions.question: What does RLHF stand for in LLM alignment?

options.text: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
Real-time Logic with Hardware Filtering
Recursive Language Heuristics Framework
Relational Learning with Hyperparameter Tuning

questions.explanation: RLHF stands for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, steering model outputs to match human preferences.

questions.question: What are the '3 Hs' of AI alignment popularized by Anthropic?

options.text: Helpful, Honest, Harmless
Heavy, High-speed, Heuristic
Hardware, Hybrid, Hostile
Human-level, Hyper-parameterized, High-yield

questions.explanation: The 3 Hs characterize desirable aligned assistant behavior: being Helpful, Honest, and Harmless.

questions.question: In traditional RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017 / InstructGPT), what is the role of the Reward Model?

options.text: To generate random prompt questions
To predict a scalar reward score indicating human preference given a prompt and candidate response
To punish users who ask difficult questions
To measure GPU thermal temperature

questions.explanation: A reward model is trained on human pairwise preference comparisons to assign scalar scores to model generations.

questions.question: Which reinforcement learning algorithm was predominantly used in early RLHF pipelines (e.g., InstructGPT, ChatGPT)?

options.text: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
Q-Learning (tabular)
SARSA
Monte Carlo Tree Search with Minimax only

questions.explanation: PPO is the policy gradient algorithm widely used to update language model policy weights based on reward model feedback.

questions.question: Why is a KL-divergence penalty added to the RLHF optimization objective?

options.text: To speed up network data transfer rates
To prevent the policy model from drifting too far from the initial SFT model and exploiting the reward model ('reward hacking')
To force the model to output shorter answers
To prevent the model from using English words

questions.explanation: The KL penalty D_KL(pi_theta || pi_ref) prevents 'reward hacking' where the model produces gibberish that tricks the reward model.

questions.question: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO, Rafailov et al., 2023) improves upon standard RLHF by:

options.text: Deriving a closed-form substitution that optimizes the policy directly on preference data without training a separate reward model or using RL loops
Adding 10 additional reward models in an ensemble
Replacing neural networks with decision trees
Requiring 100x more GPU clusters

questions.explanation: DPO mathematically reparameterizes the reward model in terms of the policy, allowing direct cross-entropy optimization on preference pairs.

questions.question: In preference datasets for alignment, each training instance typically consists of:

options.text: A prompt, a chosen (preferred) response, and a rejected (dispreferred) response
A single word and its dictionary definition
An image and its RGB pixel coordinates
A Python compiler error log

questions.explanation: Preference pairs consist of a prompt x along with a chosen response y_w and a rejected response y_l.

questions.question: What is 'Jailbreaking' in the context of aligned LLMs?

options.text: Rooting an iPhone using iOS exploits
Crafting adversarial prompts that bypass safety guardrails and force the model to generate prohibited content
Running an LLM on an unsupported operating system
Cracking the encryption of the model checkpoint

questions.explanation: Jailbreaking uses adversarial framing, roleplay, or encoding to trick safety-aligned models into violating policy.

questions.question: What is 'Sycophancy' in aligned language models?

options.text: The tendency of a model to agree with the user's stated opinion or bias, even when factually incorrect
The model speaking only in ancient Greek
The model crashing when handling numeric tables
The model refusing to reply to polite greetings

questions.explanation: Sycophancy refers to models tailoring answers to flatter or confirm user prejudices rather than stating objective truths.

questions.question: What is Constitutional AI (RLAIF) developed by Anthropic?

options.text: A legal system where judges are replaced with LLMs
An alignment method where the model critiques and refines its own responses using a written set of principles (a constitution) rather than human feedback
A method to train models only on national constitutions
A government law mandating open weights for all models

questions.explanation: Constitutional AI replaces human feedback loops with AI feedback guided by written behavioral principles and self-critiques.

questions.question: KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization) differs from DPO by:

options.text: Aligning models directly using unpaired binary feedback (thumbs up / thumbs down) inspired by behavioral prospect theory
Requiring 10-way ranking tournaments
Using exclusively quadratic regression
Excluding all safety guidelines

questions.explanation: KTO operates on unpaired signal data (whether an individual response is desirable or undesirable) using prospect theory principles.

questions.question: What is 'Reward Hacking' or 'Goodhart's Law' in AI alignment?

options.text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — the model finds degenerate ways to maximize the reward model score without fulfilling the true intent
When hackers steal the model weights from the server
When human annotators demand higher wages
When the training loss hits exactly zero

questions.explanation: Reward hacking occurs when policies optimize proxy rewards via unintended loopholes (e.g., generating repetitive pleasantries).

questions.question: What is 'Zero-Shot' prompting?

options.text: Feeding zero tokens to the model and expecting output
Asking the model to perform a task with instructions only, without providing any input-output examples
Training the model from scratch with zero parameters
Running an LLM with zero electrical power

questions.explanation: Zero-shot prompting gives the model a direct instruction or question without supplying demonstration examples.

questions.question: Few-Shot prompting (In-Context Learning) involves:

options.text: Fine-tuning model weights with backpropagation on 3 examples
Providing a few input-output demonstration examples directly within the context window prompt
Prompting the model only 3 times a day
Deleting few layers from the transformer model

questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting provides exemplars inside the prompt context to steer format and task behavior without updating model weights.

questions.question: What is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022)?

options.text: Connecting multiple GPUs in a daisy chain
Prompting the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before arriving at a final answer ('Let's think step by step')
Encrypting prompts with blockchain hashes
Limiting the model to generating only one word at a time

questions.explanation: Chain-of-Thought prompting induces explicit reasoning trajectories, significantly improving multi-step math and logic solving.

questions.question: What is the 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon in long-context LLMs (Liu et al., 2023)?

options.text: Models fail to download middle chapters of books
LLMs retrieve and reason over information located at the beginning or end of long prompts far better than information in the middle
Middle-aged engineers write poorer prompts
Transformers skip attention for tokens located in the middle of a sentence

questions.explanation: Empirical studies show LLM performance degrades severely when relevant facts are situated in the middle of long context windows.

questions.question: What is Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) prompting framework?

options.text: Generating a single linear paragraph of text
Exploring multiple reasoning paths over tree-like decision structures with lookahead and backtracking
Converting text into binary search trees for sorting
Using Decision Trees instead of Deep Neural Networks

questions.explanation: Tree-of-Thoughts allows models to deliberate over multiple distinct reasoning branches, evaluate progress, and backtrack.

questions.question: What is Prompt Injection?

options.text: A security vulnerability where untrusted external user input manipulates the LLM into ignoring system instructions and executing rogue commands
Inserting SQL queries into database tables directly
Injecting electrical signals into GPU transistors
Updating system RAM with faster DDR5 memory

questions.explanation: Prompt injection occurs when user data overrides developer system prompts to hijack model behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?

options.text: Direct injection comes from the user prompt; indirect injection enters via external data ingested by the model (e.g., a poisoned webpage or email)
Direct injection uses Python; indirect injection uses C++
Direct injection is harmless; indirect injection breaks the hardware
There is no difference

questions.explanation: Indirect prompt injection occurs when third-party content (e.g., retrieved web text or PDF) contains hidden hostile instructions.

questions.question: How does Self-Consistency decoding improve reasoning in LLMs (Wang et al., 2022)?

options.text: By forcing the model temperature to zero
By sampling multiple diverse CoT reasoning paths with nonzero temperature and taking the majority vote answer
By asking the model if it is confident in its answer
By retraining the model on its own outputs

questions.explanation: Self-consistency generates multiple stochastic reasoning paths and selects the consensus answer via marginalization/majority voting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'System Prompt' in ChatML and modern chat APIs?

options.text: To tell the computer operating system which port to open
To set foundational behavioral guardrails, persona, tone, and operational boundaries for the conversation
To compile Python scripts before running them
To configure user billing details

questions.explanation: System prompts establish persistent instructions and persona constraints governing assistant behavior throughout the session.

questions.question: Which decoding parameter controls the randomness of token selection by scaling logits prior to softmax?

options.text: Temperature
Learning Rate
Batch Size
Weight Decay

questions.explanation: Temperature scales logits (z_i / T); higher T flattens the distribution for creative diversity, while T->0 approaches greedy decoding.

questions.question: What does Top-p (Nucleus) sampling do?

options.text: Samples only from the top p% of all model weights
Samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds threshold p
Samples exactly p tokens per sentence
Rejects any token containing the letter 'p'

questions.explanation: Nucleus sampling dynamically cuts off the long tail of low-probability tokens by truncating when cumulative sum reaches p.

questions.question: What is ReAct (Reason + Act) prompting framework (Yao et al., 2022)?

options.text: A JavaScript UI framework for displaying chatbots
A paradigm combining reasoning traces (thoughts) and task-specific actions (e.g., API calls, searches) in an interleaved loop
A method to suppress all emotional words in responses
A technique to compile React components using Python

questions.explanation: ReAct interleaves reasoning ('Thought') with action ('Action: Search[...]') and observations to solve complex interactive tasks.

questions.question: What is 'hallucination' in the context of Large Language Models?

options.text: When the model experiences hardware GPU thermal overthrottling
When the model generates plausible-sounding statements that are factually false, unfaithful, or unsupported by evidence
When the user hallucinates while reading responses
When the model outputs text in colorful fonts

questions.explanation: Hallucination occurs when an LLM produces confident, coherent, yet factually untrue or fabricated assertions.

questions.question: What is the MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) benchmark used for?

options.text: Measuring GPU memory bandwidth during training
Evaluating cross-domain knowledge and reasoning across 57 subjects ranging from elementary math to professional law and medicine
Testing optical character recognition on scanned PDFs
Benchmarking audio transcription accuracy

questions.explanation: MMLU is an industry-standard benchmark spanning 57 academic subjects to measure general knowledge and reasoning.

questions.question: What does GSM8K benchmark test?

options.text: Grammar and spelling metrics in 8,000 documents
Grade school math multi-step word problem reasoning
Global social media sentiment trends
Speech recognition on 8,000 audio clips

questions.explanation: GSM8K comprises 8,500 grade school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic and natural language reasoning.

questions.question: HumanEval benchmark developed by OpenAI evaluates:

options.text: Functional correctness of Python code generation based on unit test pass rates (pass@k)
Human emotional intelligence during therapy chat
Medical diagnosis accuracy on radiology images
Grammatical correctness of poetry translations

questions.explanation: HumanEval evaluates code synthesis on 164 Python coding challenges verified by rigorous unit test execution.

questions.question: What is 'LLM-as-a-Judge' evaluation methodology (e.g., MT-Bench, AlpacaEval)?

options.text: Appointing neural networks as judges in civil courtrooms
Using a strong frontier LLM (e.g., GPT-4) to grade and compare model responses against reference criteria or pairwise baselines
Letting the model write its own evaluation benchmarks
Grading models based on line count of generated text

questions.explanation: LLM-as-a-Judge employs high-capability models to evaluate quality, coherence, and instruction following at scale.

questions.question: Which bias is common when using LLM-as-a-Judge for pairwise evaluations?

options.text: Position bias (preferring whichever candidate response is presented first)
Verbosity bias (preferring longer, more verbose responses regardless of quality)
Self-enhancement bias (preferring responses generated by the judge's own model family)
All of the above

questions.explanation: LLM judges exhibit well-documented biases including position bias, verbosity bias, and self-preference bias.

questions.question: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic hallucination in summarization tasks?

options.text: Intrinsic directly contradicts information in the source document; extrinsic introduces claims that cannot be verified from the source
Intrinsic is harmless; extrinsic causes hardware errors
Intrinsic happens on GPUs; extrinsic happens on CPUs
There is no difference

questions.explanation: Intrinsic hallucination asserts facts conflicting with the prompt text; extrinsic hallucination adds unverifiable outside facts.

questions.question: Why is exact-string match accuracy (EM) inadequate for evaluating open-ended generative tasks?

options.text: Because valid answers can be phrased in thousands of semantically equivalent variations not matching the single ground truth string
Because computers cannot compare strings
Because EM is computationally impossible on GPUs
Because open-ended tasks only generate images

questions.explanation: Language allows infinite paraphrasing; an accurate answer may not match the exact reference characters.

questions.question: What is BOLD (Bias in Open-Ended Language Generation Dataset) designed to evaluate?

options.text: Model generation speed across server locations
Fairness and demographic biases across gender, race, religion, and professions
The maximum token length supported by attention layers
The financial cost of running API calls

questions.explanation: BOLD benchmarks social bias and representation across diverse demographic domains in open-ended generation.

questions.question: What does the 'pass@k' metric measure in code and formal generation benchmarks?

options.text: The probability that at least one of the k generated candidate samples passes all unit test testcases
The percentage of students who pass a computer science exam
The number of tokens generated per millisecond
The percentage of lines that contain comments

questions.explanation: pass@k calculates the probability that among k independently sampled code solutions, at least one passes unit tests.

questions.question: What is TruthfulQA benchmark specifically constructed to measure?

options.text: How fast a model can search Google
How often a model mimics human falsehoods, common myths, and conspiracy theories versus stating verified facts
The quantum physics proficiency of models
The grammar accuracy in Shakespearean plays

questions.explanation: TruthfulQA tests whether language models mimic widespread human superstitions, false beliefs, and conspiracy theories.

questions.question: Which mitigation technique significantly reduces factual hallucination in factual query answering?

options.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounding responses in retrieved authoritative documents
Increasing temperature to 2.0
Deleting system prompts completely
Disabling attention layers

questions.explanation: RAG anchors model generation in external, retrieved factual evidence, drastically reducing ungrounded hallucinations.

questions.question: What is the core architecture of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?

options.text: Fine-tuning a billion parameter model on every single user query
Retrieving relevant documents from an external knowledge store and passing them as context inside the LLM prompt
Storing all company data directly inside transformer neural weights
Using speech synthesis to read text out loud

questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant external documents via vector search and includes them in the context prompt for grounded generation.

questions.question: In vector search for RAG, what metric is most commonly used to compute similarity between dense embeddings?

options.text: Cosine Similarity (or inner dot product of normalized vectors)
Hamming distance on ASCII strings
Levenshtein edit distance
Mean Absolute Error

questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two dense semantic embedding vectors in latent space.

questions.question: What is 'Chunking' in a RAG ingestion pipeline?

options.text: Throwing away 50% of files at random
Breaking large documents into smaller, semantically coherent segments suitable for embedding and context retrieval
Renaming files with numeric prefixes
Translating text into hexadecimal strings

questions.explanation: Chunking divides large text corpora into manageable pieces that respect embedding model token limits and optimize retrieval focus.

questions.question: What is a Vector Database (e.g., Pinecone, Chroma, Milvus, Qdrant)?

options.text: A relational database that only accepts SVG vector images
A specialized database designed for indexing, storing, and fast nearest-neighbor search over high-dimensional vector embeddings
A spreadsheet software like Microsoft Excel
A hardware processor inside GPU clusters

questions.explanation: Vector databases index high-dimensional embeddings to perform ultra-fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval.

questions.question: How does HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) improve vector search performance?

options.text: By performing brute-force exact comparison across all billion vectors
By building a multi-layer graph index for fast approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search with logarithmic time complexity
By compressing all text into 1-bit integers
By deleting 90% of index nodes

questions.explanation: HNSW organizes vector indices into hierarchical skip-list graphs to deliver fast approximate nearest neighbor search.

questions.question: What is Hybrid Search in modern RAG systems?

options.text: Searching across both desktop and mobile devices
Combining dense semantic retrieval (vector embeddings) with sparse keyword retrieval (BM25) using reciprocal rank fusion
Searching text and audio files simultaneously
Using two different web browsers

questions.explanation: Hybrid search fuses sparse lexical search (BM25 for exact codes/names) and dense semantic vectors for optimal recall.

questions.question: What is the function of a Cross-Encoder Reranker in an advanced RAG pipeline?

options.text: To embed documents into vector databases
To jointly score the query and each candidate passage through full cross-attention to re-order the top retrieved chunks accurately
To translate English documents into foreign languages
To encrypt user search queries

questions.explanation: Rerankers apply joint cross-attention over (query, document) pairs to dramatically refine the relevance ranking of candidates.

questions.question: What is 'Tool Calling' or 'Function Calling' in agentic LLMs?

options.text: The LLM generating a structured output (like JSON) specifying a function name and arguments to invoke an external API or tool
The LLM calling a telephone customer service representative
A programmer calling the LLM from a Python terminal
A hardware crash error code

questions.explanation: Tool calling enables models to output structured invocation payloads (e.g., function name, args) to execute external software tools.

questions.question: In an autonomous agent loop, what are the core components often structured around?

options.text: Planning, Memory, Tool Use, and Reflection/Action Execution
Accounting, Payroll, Shipping, and Invoicing
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Webpack
Microphone, Speaker, Monitor, and Keyboard

questions.explanation: AI agents integrate planning (decomposition), memory (short-term context & long-term vector retrieval), tools, and self-reflection.

questions.question: What does the 'Self-Refine' pattern enable in an LLM agent workflow?

options.text: The agent generates an initial draft, critiques its own output against constraints, and iteratively rewrites to improve quality
The agent shuts itself down after 5 minutes
The agent deletes user prompt history
The agent asks for financial compensation

questions.explanation: Self-Refine allows agents to iteratively inspect intermediate work product, identify flaws, and rewrite improved versions.

questions.question: What is the primary vulnerability of Naive RAG without reranking or metadata filtering?

options.text: Retrieving irrelevant or noisy chunks that distract the LLM, introduce conflicting information, or trigger hallucination
Overheating the computer motherboard
Exceeding the maximum RAM of the internet
Accidental deletion of source database files

questions.explanation: Naive semantic retrieval can pull irrelevant chunks that pollute context, causing the LLM to synthesize flawed or distracted answers.

questions.question: What is Multi-Agent Collaboration (e.g., AutoGen, CrewAI)?

options.text: Multiple humans writing prompts simultaneously
Multiple specialized LLM agents assuming distinct roles (e.g., researcher, coder, reviewer) and conversing to solve complex multi-step tasks
Running the same LLM on two different computers
A software license allowing multiple users

questions.explanation: Multi-agent frameworks coordinate specialized agents with unique personas and toolkits to cooperatively accomplish complex goals.

questions.question: How does HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings) enhance dense passage retrieval in RAG?

options.text: By asking the LLM to generate a hypothetical answer to the query first, then using that document's embedding to search for real passages
By deleting questions that have no answers
By indexing only fictional novels
By encrypting document vectors with private keys

questions.explanation: HyDE generates a zero-shot pseudo-document to bridge semantic distance between concise queries and long factual passages.

questions.question: What is GraphRAG and how does it advance conventional vector-based chunk retrieval?

options.text: It relies solely on pie charts and bar graphs
It constructs knowledge graphs of entities and relationships across documents to answer complex global, multi-hop queries
It replaces LLMs with graphics processing units
It limits retrieval to image files only

questions.explanation: GraphRAG extracts semantic entities and community summaries into knowledge graphs, excelling at holistic sensemaking questions.

questions.question: In agentic workflows, what is the role of a state graph (as in LangGraph)?

options.text: To track and persist agent memory, decision nodes, tool results, and conditional routing over multi-turn cycles
To draw flowchart diagrams on the user's screen
To monitor GPU fan speeds
To terminate network connections when errors occur

questions.explanation: State graphs define cyclic workflows where agent states evolve, branch conditionally, and loop until tasks finish.
